title: Token Development & ERC Standards
tagline: ERC-20, ERC-721, ERC-1155 and ERC-4626, with tokenomics, vesting, airdrops and a responsible launch
summary: Build tokens the professional way: understand the ledger inside a token contract, assemble ERC-20 tokens with OpenZeppelin, add permit, voting and vesting, learn ERC-721, ERC-1155 and ERC-4626, design tokenomics and a Merkle airdrop, and plan an honest, secure launch. All Solidity listings were compiled with solc 0.8 against OpenZeppelin 5. This course gives education, not legal or investment advice.

modules.title: Token fundamentals
modules.summary: What a token is, how fungible and non-fungible tokens differ, the ERC-20 interface and how decimals work.
modules.outcome: You can explain what a token is, choose between the main standards and convert between human and stored amounts.
modules.intro: A token is not a coin with its own blockchain. It is a smart contract that keeps a table of who owns how much. This module explains that idea, introduces the standards that make tokens work everywhere and shows why decimals trip up so many beginners.

topics.title: A token is a ledger inside a contract
topics.html:
When you hold a token such as a stable-value payment token, your wallet does not contain coins. A smart contract keeps a table, a mapping from addresses to numbers, and your balance is the number stored next to your address. To send tokens, you call a function that subtracts from your row and adds to the recipient's row. That is the whole idea.

The parts of the contract
PartRole
balanceOf mappingThe ledger: address to amount
totalSupplyThe sum of all balances
transferMove your own tokens
approve and allowanceLet another address spend up to a limit
transferFromSpend tokens on someone's behalf, using an allowance
Transfer and Approval eventsLet wallets and explorers track activity
decimalsHow many decimal places to show
Definition

Token standard. An agreed set of function names and behaviour, such as ERC-20, so that every wallet, exchange and app can work with any token that follows it without custom code.

Check what you just learned

1. Where is a token balance actually stored?
  • In your wallet app
  • In a bank
  • On your phone
  • In a mapping inside the token's smart contract (correct)

The contract is the ledger.

Check what you just learned

1. A wallet shows your token balance by:
  • Asking the contract for balanceOf (correct)
  • Holding coins
  • Calling your bank
  • Mining

It reads the contract.
keyPoints: A token is a ledger kept by a smart contract.
Standards make tokens work in every wallet and app.

topics.title: Fungible, non-fungible and multi-token standards
topics.html:
The main families
StandardItems are...Typical use
ERC-20Fungible: every unit is identical and interchangeableCurrencies, points, stablecoins, governance tokens
ERC-721Non-fungible: each token id is uniqueCertificates, tickets, collectibles, property records
ERC-1155Multi-token: fungible and non-fungible items in one contractGames, large collections, batch transfers
ERC-4626A vault whose shares are ERC-20 tokensYield pools, savings, lending shares
ERC-2612ERC-20 with approvals by signature (permit)Gasless approvals

Pick the simplest standard that fits. A loyalty currency does not need unique ids, and a certificate should not be an interchangeable coin. Using a familiar standard also means that wallets, explorers and other developers already know how your token behaves.

Check what you just learned

1. Which standard fits a course certificate unique to each graduate?
  • ERC-20
  • ERC-721 (correct)
  • ERC-4626
  • ERC-2612

A unique token for each person.

Tip

Always say what a token is for before choosing a standard. Many projects do not need a token at all.

Check what you just learned

1. Interchangeable units point to:
  • A database
  • ERC-721
  • ERC-20 (correct)
  • A photo

Fungible tokens.
keyPoints: ERC-20 is fungible, ERC-721 unique, ERC-1155 mixed, ERC-4626 vault shares.
Choose the simplest standard that fits the job.

topics.title: Decimals and units
topics.html:
The contract can store only whole numbers. To represent fractions, tokens agree that the stored number is a multiple of a tiny base unit. With 18 decimals, which most tokens use, the amount 1.0 is stored as 1,000,000,000,000,000,000. With 6 decimals, as some payment tokens use, 1.0 is stored as 1,000,000. The decimals value is only a hint for display: the contract itself works only with the raw whole numbers.

Examples
Human amountDecimalsStored value
1181,000,000,000,000,000,000
0.518500,000,000,000,000,000
2,500.562,500,500,000
101

Decimals converter

Change the human amount and the decimals to see the stored number. A teaching tool: very large numbers are rounded here.

Adjust Human amount, Decimals and see Stored whole number, Smallest possible unit (tokens) change.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing tokens with different decimals in one calculation without converting.
  • Assuming every token has 18 decimals.
  • Writing 100 when you meant 100 × 10^decimals in code or scripts.

Check what you just learned

1. A token with 6 decimals stores 1.0 as:
  • 1
  • 1,000
  • 1e18
  • 1,000,000 (correct)

10 to the power of 6.

Check what you just learned

1. With 18 decimals, 1 token is stored as:
  • 10^18 (correct)
  • 1
  • 18
  • 0

A very large whole number.

Key terms: flip and sort

Token
An entry in a smart contract's ledger
Fungible
Every unit is identical
Non-fungible
Each item is unique
ERC-20
The standard for fungible tokens
Decimals
How many places to show
Base unit
The smallest indivisible amount
keyPoints: Contracts store whole numbers; decimals are a display hint.
Always convert when tokens have different decimals.

modules.title: Building ERC-20 tokens
modules.summary: Using OpenZeppelin to build capped, burnable, mintable tokens, and understanding allowances and their risks.
modules.outcome: You can build a capped, burnable token with OpenZeppelin and explain the approve and transferFrom flow and its dangers.
modules.intro: Writing a token from scratch is a good lesson and a bad idea for production. Professionals build on audited libraries. This module shows how to assemble a real token in a few lines and how allowances work, since they are behind many wallet-draining scams.

topics.title: Assembling a token with OpenZeppelin
topics.html:
What each piece gives you
PieceAdds
ERC20Balances, transfers, allowances and events, written and audited by others
ERC20Burnableburn and burnFrom so holders can destroy their own tokens
ERC20CappedA hard limit on total supply that cannot be exceeded
OwnableA single owner address that can call onlyOwner functions
_update overrideRequired because both ERC20 and ERC20Capped hook into transfers; you must say how they combine

Notice what the owner can and cannot do: mint up to the cap and nothing else. They cannot take tokens from anyone or freeze balances. Limiting powers like this is what lets holders trust a token. Every power you add must be justified, disclosed and protected.

Check what you just learned

1. What does ERC20Capped guarantee?
  • Free gas
  • Total supply can never exceed the cap (correct)
  • No one can sell
  • Faster blocks

A hard limit.

Watch out

Use the official OpenZeppelin Contracts Wizard or documentation for your version. Libraries change between major versions, so copy-pasting old code can break or, worse, compile with different behaviour.

Check what you just learned

1. Why override _update in CampusCoin?
  • To rename it
  • To save gas
  • Two parents hook into transfers (correct)
  • Because it is required for events

Solidity needs you to resolve the conflict.
keyPoints: Build on audited libraries; combine small extensions.
Keep owner powers as small as the design allows.

topics.title: Allowances: the approve and transferFrom flow
topics.html:
Why allowances are risky
RiskExplanationSafer habit
Unlimited approvalsMany apps ask for 'infinite' allowance for convenience; if that app is hacked, all your tokens of that kind are exposedApprove only what you need
Fake sitesA scam page asks you to approve its contract and then drains the tokensCheck the address and the website; read the wallet prompt
Old approvalsAllowances stay open until you change themReview and revoke old ones
Allowance raceChanging an allowance from 50 to 30 can be front-run so the spender uses bothSet to zero first, or use increase and decrease functions or permit

As a developer you must treat the user's approval as a loan of trust. Pull only the amount you will use, never ask for more than the action needs, and explain it in your interface. As a user, remember that signing an approval can be as dangerous as handing over your wallet for one token.

Check what you just learned

1. Why are unlimited approvals risky?
  • They cost more gas
  • They expire quickly
  • They are slower
  • If the spender is compromised, all those tokens can be taken (correct)

Limit what you approve.

Check what you just learned

1. A safer approval is:
  • Only the amount needed (correct)
  • Unlimited always
  • Another wallet's key
  • None ever

Limit exposure.
keyPoints: approve sets an allowance; transferFrom spends it.
Unlimited and forgotten approvals are common drain risks.

topics.title: Testing and deploying a token
topics.html:
What to test

  1. Total supply after construction equals the initial mint.
  2. transfer reduces the sender and increases the receiver by exactly the same amount.
  3. A transfer above the balance reverts.
  4. transferFrom fails without an allowance and reduces the allowance when it succeeds.
  5. Minting above the cap reverts, and only the owner can mint.
  6. burn reduces both balance and total supply.
  7. Events are emitted with the right values.
Deployment checklist
StepWhy
Deploy first to a test networkPractise with no real value
Verify the source code on a block explorerAnyone can read what the contract does
Check the owner and roles after deploymentPowers must be where you intended
Move the owner to a multi-signature walletSingle-key risk
Publish the contract address on your official site onlyUsers can avoid fake tokens
Document the parametersName, symbol, decimals, cap and admin powers

A test suite that covers these cases takes an hour to write and can save a project. Fuzz tests that send random amounts are especially good at finding arithmetic edge cases.

Check what you just learned

1. Why verify the source code on an explorer?
  • It lowers gas
  • Anyone can inspect exactly what the deployed contract does (correct)
  • It hides the code
  • It is required to deploy

Transparency builds trust.

Check what you just learned

1. A transfer above the balance should:
  • Succeed
  • Mint tokens
  • Revert (correct)
  • Burn tokens

The call must fail.

Key terms: flip and sort

OpenZeppelin
A library of audited contracts
Cap
A maximum total supply
Burn
Permanently destroy tokens
Allowance
How much a spender may use
Verified source
Published code matching the deployed contract
Owner
An address with special powers
keyPoints: Test supply, transfers, allowances, minting, burning and events.
Verify the source and publish the address officially.

modules.title: Advanced token features
modules.summary: Permit signatures, voting power, owner powers and their risks, and vesting contracts.
modules.outcome: You can add permit and voting features, judge owner powers critically and build a linear vesting schedule.
modules.intro: Real tokens often need more than transfers: governance, gasless approvals, time-locked grants and sometimes emergency controls. Each feature is useful and each adds risk. This module shows how to add them thoughtfully.

topics.title: Permit and voting power
topics.html:
Two useful extensions
ExtensionWhat it doesWhy it matters
ERC20PermitA holder signs an off-chain message that approves a spender; the spender submits itNo separate approval transaction, so a smoother experience and lower cost
ERC20VotesTracks voting power with checkpoints and lets holders delegateGovernance can count balances at a past block, preventing last-minute vote buying

Delegation lets a holder give their voting power to themself or another address. Tokens that are not delegated have no voting power in this design, so users must delegate (even to themselves) to take part.

Check what you just learned

1. What does permit let a user do?
  • Mint tokens
  • Change decimals
  • Freeze tokens
  • Approve a spender by signing a message instead of sending a transaction (correct)

A signed approval.

Watch out

Signed approvals are powerful. Wallets should show exactly what is being approved, and users should refuse requests they do not understand.

Check what you just learned

1. ERC20Votes helps governance by:
  • Counting balances at a past block (correct)
  • Lowering gas
  • Hiding votes
  • Minting tokens

Checkpoints.
keyPoints: Permit allows approvals by signature.
Votes tracks historical voting power and delegation.

topics.title: Owner powers and honest design
topics.html:
Common owner powers
PowerWhy a team wants itRisk to holders
Unlimited mintingFlexibilityDilution of everyone
Freezing accountsCompliance or theft responseFunds can be locked arbitrarily
Pausing transfersEmergency stopTrading can be halted
Changing feesFunding the projectFees raised to a punishing level
Upgrading the contractFixing bugsRules can change completely

Questions a careful buyer or reviewer asks

  1. Who holds each power: one person, or several through a multi-signature wallet?
  2. Is there a time-lock so holders can react?
  3. Are the powers limited in size (a fee cap, a mint cap)?
  4. Are they publicly documented?
  5. Are they truly necessary for the stated purpose?

For your own designs, apply the same test: give the project only the powers it genuinely needs, cap them, put them behind several keys and a delay, and write them down. A token with no owner powers is the simplest to trust but also the hardest to fix.

Check what you just learned

1. Why can unlimited owner minting be harmful?
  • It costs gas
  • It can dilute every holder's share (correct)
  • It is slow
  • It hides balances

More tokens, smaller share.

Check what you just learned

1. A time-lock on owner actions gives holders:
  • Faster blocks
  • Free tokens
  • Time to react (correct)
  • Anonymity

Notice before change.
keyPoints: Every owner power is a risk to holders.
Limit, cap, delay and disclose powers.

topics.title: Vesting contracts
topics.html:
Vesting calculator

Change the months elapsed to see the released amount for a 1,200,000 token grant over 48 months once the 12-month cliff has passed.

Adjust Months elapsed (after the cliff has passed) and see Released tokens change.

Common mistakes

  • Locking tokens in a vesting contract with no way to check the schedule publicly.
  • Giving the admin the ability to cancel without notice or limits.
  • Forgetting that the contract must hold the full amount before vesting starts.

Check what you just learned

1. What does a cliff do?
  • Releases everything at once
  • Doubles the grant
  • Burns tokens
  • Releases nothing until a date, then starts vesting (correct)

A waiting period.

Check what you just learned

1. Why vest team tokens?
  • To align incentives over time (correct)
  • To save gas
  • To hide them
  • To burn them

Long-term commitment.

Key terms: flip and sort

Permit
Approval by signature
Delegation
Giving voting power to an address
Checkpoint
A recorded balance at a point in time
Cliff
A period before any tokens vest
Vesting
Gradual release over time
Time-lock
A delay before a change takes effect
keyPoints: Vesting releases tokens gradually, optionally after a cliff.
A public, audited vesting contract builds trust.

modules.title: Beyond ERC-20: NFTs, multi-tokens and vaults
modules.summary: ERC-721, ERC-1155 and ERC-4626: what each is for, how to build them and where they go wrong.
modules.outcome: You can build simple ERC-721, ERC-1155 and ERC-4626 contracts and choose between them.
modules.intro: Not everything is a currency. Certificates, tickets, in-game items and savings pools each have their own standard. Learning them widens the range of problems you can solve and prepares you for the next courses on NFTs, DeFi and applications.

topics.title: ERC-721: unique tokens
topics.html:
Key ERC-721 ideas
IdeaMeaning
Token idEach token has a unique number inside the contract
ownerOf(id)Exactly one owner per token
safeTransferFromChecks that a contract recipient can handle NFTs, avoiding tokens stuck forever
tokenURIA link to metadata: name, description and image
ApprovalsPer-token approval and approve-for-all, the latter being a major scam vector

Where the image lives matters. The token holds a pointer, not the image. If the pointer is a normal web address and the website disappears, the NFT will show nothing. Content-addressed storage reduces that risk, and the design should say clearly what is stored on the chain and what is not.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use safeMint and safeTransferFrom?
  • They are cheaper
  • They check that a receiving contract can handle NFTs (correct)
  • They hide ids
  • They are required for events

Avoid stuck tokens.

Check what you just learned

1. ERC-721 ownerOf returns:
  • The price
  • The cap
  • The single owner of a token id (correct)
  • The creator's name

One owner per id.
keyPoints: ERC-721 gives each token a unique id and one owner.
Metadata lives off-chain; plan where.

topics.title: ERC-1155: many kinds in one contract
topics.html:
Why games and large collections like ERC-1155
FeatureBenefit
One contract, many idsCheaper than deploying a contract per item
Fungible and unique togetherId 1 can have millions of copies, id 2 only one
Batch transfer and balance functionsSend many item types in one transaction
Shared metadata templateA URI pattern with {id} covers every item

The trade-off is that many marketplaces and tools support ERC-721 more fully than ERC-1155, and per-item features such as royalties and approvals need extra care. Choose the standard that matches the way the items will really be used.

Check what you just learned

1. Which design suits a game with coins and one-of-a-kind swords?
  • Many ERC-20 contracts
  • ERC-4626
  • A spreadsheet
  • ERC-1155 (correct)

Mixed items in one contract.

Check what you just learned

1. In ERC-1155, id 1 with 1,000 copies is:
  • Fungible (correct)
  • Unique
  • Impossible
  • Burned

Copies are interchangeable.
keyPoints: ERC-1155 handles fungible and unique items in one contract.
It supports efficient batch operations.

topics.title: ERC-4626: tokenised vaults
topics.html:
Why a standard vault interface matters
Without itWith ERC-4626
Each protocol invents its own deposit and withdraw functionsdeposit, mint, withdraw, redeem and convert functions are the same everywhere
Integrators write custom code per vaultWallets, aggregators and other protocols can plug in any vault
Watch out

Vaults have a known attack: if the first depositor can manipulate the share price (an 'inflation' attack), later depositors may lose funds to rounding. The library includes mitigations, but you must understand and test them.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a vault share?
  • A loan
  • An ERC-20 token representing a part of the pool (correct)
  • A signature
  • A cap

Shares track a portion of assets.

Check what you just learned

1. When a vault earns yield, each share becomes:
  • Worthless
  • Worth less
  • Worth more (correct)
  • Unique

Same shares, more assets.

Key terms: flip and sort

NFT
A non-fungible token
ERC-721
The standard for unique tokens
ERC-1155
The multi-token standard
ERC-4626
The tokenised vault standard
Metadata
Descriptive data for a token, usually off-chain
Share
A token representing part of a pool
keyPoints: ERC-4626 standardises deposit, redeem and share conversion.
Rounding and share-price manipulation are the main risks.

modules.title: Tokenomics and distribution
modules.summary: Supply design, allocation, airdrops with Merkle proofs and warning signs in token economies.
modules.outcome: You can design a fair allocation table, build a Merkle airdrop and recognise unhealthy token economies.
modules.intro: Code decides what a token can do; tokenomics decides who ends up with it and why anyone cares. Weak or unfair distribution can ruin a technically perfect token. This module covers designing allocations, handing tokens out efficiently and spotting trouble.

topics.title: Supply and allocation
topics.html:
Questions of supply design
QuestionConsiderations
Fixed or growing supply?Fixed supply is simple and predictable; growing supply needs rules and limits
How is new supply created?Mining rewards, earning rules or governance-approved minting
Can supply shrink?Burning can reduce supply; explain who does it and why
Who holds what?A fair, publicly documented allocation
When can they sell?Vesting schedules, cliffs and locks
A sample allocation
GroupShareRationale
Community and rewards40%Released gradually to those who contribute
Team15%Vests over four years
Investors15%Vests with a cliff
Treasury20%Spent by public vote
Liquidity10%Enables trading in a fair way

Allocation explorer

Change the supply and the team and investor shares to see how many tokens insiders hold. A teaching tool.

Adjust Total supply, Team %, Investors % and see Insider percentage, Insider tokens change.

Check what you just learned

1. Why publish the allocation table?
  • To impress
  • It lowers gas
  • It is required by the compiler
  • So holders can judge how concentrated the supply is (correct)

Transparency enables trust.

Check what you just learned

1. A healthy allocation is usually:
  • Documented and gradual (correct)
  • Concentrated in a few wallets
  • Secret
  • Unlimited

Transparent and fair.
keyPoints: Design supply, creation, burning and allocation deliberately.
Publish who holds what and when they can sell.

topics.title: Airdrops and Merkle proofs
topics.html:
Sending tokens to 20,000 addresses costs the project a transaction for each. A Merkle airdrop stores one 32-byte root and lets each recipient pay for their own claim. Only the people who really want the tokens bother to claim, and the project's cost stays small.

Design choices for airdrops
ChoiceConsideration
EligibilityBe clear and fair; guard against fake accounts
DeadlineAllow unclaimed tokens to return to the treasury after a published date
AmountAvoid dust, which can cost more in gas than it is worth
CommunicationOfficial channels only, because scammers imitate airdrops
Law and taxDistribution may have legal consequences that vary by country

Check what you just learned

1. Why does a Merkle airdrop save the project money?
  • It skips verification
  • It stores one root instead of sending to everyone (correct)
  • It pays no gas ever
  • It burns tokens

Claimants pay their own gas.

Check what you just learned

1. A Merkle proof shows that:
  • The user is rich
  • The token is valuable
  • An entry belongs to the tree with a given root (correct)
  • The code is audited

Inclusion proof.
keyPoints: A Merkle airdrop stores one root; users prove their entries.
Plan eligibility, deadlines and communication, and take legal advice.

topics.title: Warning signs and sustainable design
topics.html:
Warning signs
SignWhy it matters
Most supply held by a few anonymous walletsThey can sell and crash the price
No vesting for insidersNo long-term commitment
Guaranteed returns promisedUnrealistic and often unlawful
Unlimited owner minting or hidden feesHolders can be diluted or trapped
Pressure to buy quicklyA classic manipulation tactic
Unverified contract codeNobody can inspect what it does
No clear use for the tokenValue depends only on hype

Sustainable token design starts with a real purpose that does not depend on the price rising. If the only reason to hold a token is to sell it to someone else later, the design depends on new buyers arriving and will eventually fail. If the token gives access, voting power, payments or rewards that people value, demand has a reason to exist.

Questions to ask

  • What can someone do with this token other than sell it?
  • What happens if nobody new joins?
  • Who can change the rules?
  • Who benefits first, and who is left last?
  • Is it clear and honest about its risks?

Check what you just learned

1. Why is 'guaranteed returns' a warning sign?
  • It is boring
  • It is cheap
  • It is legal
  • No honest project can guarantee returns (correct)

It is a typical scam claim.

Watch out

This course does not give investment or legal advice. Never put in money you cannot afford to lose, and take proper advice before issuing or selling any token.

Check what you just learned

1. A token with value only from new buyers depends on:
  • Constant new buyers (correct)
  • Real use
  • Audits
  • Decimals

That design is fragile.

Key terms: flip and sort

Tokenomics
The economic design of a token
Allocation
How supply is divided among groups
Airdrop
Free distribution of tokens
Merkle root
A short hash representing a whole list
Treasury
Funds held for the project
Dilution
A smaller share caused by new supply
keyPoints: Concentration, no vesting, guaranteed returns and pressure are red flags.
Sustainable design starts with real use beyond price.

modules.title: Launching responsibly
modules.summary: Legal awareness, security preparation, honest disclosure and a launch checklist.
modules.outcome: You can write an honest risk disclosure, plan a safe launch and recognise when a token is the wrong tool.
modules.intro: Launching a token is easy; launching one responsibly is hard. Tokens can be treated as regulated financial products in some places, scams are common, and mistakes are permanent. This module covers the habits that separate serious projects from reckless ones.

topics.title: Law, regulation and honesty
topics.html:
Rules about tokens vary widely by country and change quickly. A token that is a harmless loyalty point in one place may be treated as a financial instrument in another, especially if it is sold to raise money or if buyers expect profit from the efforts of others. This course cannot tell you which rules apply to you; a qualified lawyer in the relevant place can.

Questions to take to a lawyer
QuestionWhy
Does the token have features of a security or collective investment?Triggers licensing, disclosure and restrictions
Are we selling it, giving it away or rewarding work?Different rules apply
Who may we offer it to, in which countries?Cross-border rules differ
Are there anti-money-laundering or know-your-customer duties?Some activities require identity checks
What are the tax consequences for us and for recipients?Rewards and sales can be taxable
What must we say in marketing?Misleading claims can be offences

Honest communication

  • Say plainly what the token is and is not.
  • Never promise profits or guaranteed returns.
  • Disclose who holds large amounts and what powers exist.
  • Explain the main risks, including bugs and loss of keys.
  • Do not pressure people to buy, and never target people who cannot afford losses.

Check what you just learned

1. Who can tell you which laws apply to your token?
  • Nobody
  • A qualified lawyer in the relevant place (correct)
  • A social media post
  • The compiler

Rules vary by place.

Watch out

This lesson is education, not legal advice.

Check what you just learned

1. Marketing a token should never:
  • Describe risks
  • Name the contract
  • Promise guaranteed profits (correct)
  • State the cap

Misleading claims are harmful.
keyPoints: Rules vary by country and by how a token is offered.
Speak honestly and take professional legal advice.

topics.title: Security and scam awareness
topics.html:
Scams you and your users will meet
ScamHow it worksDefence
Fake tokenA copy with the same name and a different contract addressPublish the one official address and tell users to check it
Rug pullThe creators drain the liquidity or mint endlessly and disappearLocked liquidity, capped supply, multi-signature control and transparency
HoneypotA token that can be bought but not sold, because the code blocks salesRead the code and test small; honest projects have nothing to hide
Phishing approvalA fake site asks users to approve a draining contractEducate users and never ask for unlimited approvals
ImpersonationFake support accounts offer help and ask for recovery phrasesOfficial channels only; nobody ever needs your recovery phrase

Security habits for builders

  • Use audited libraries and keep the contract small.
  • Test thoroughly, including fuzz and invariant tests.
  • Get an independent review for anything holding value.
  • Use a multi-signature wallet for owner powers.
  • Keep deployment keys on hardware wallets, never in code.
  • Publish a security contact and consider a bug bounty.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a rug pull?
  • A deployment tool
  • A fee
  • A kind of test
  • Creators draining value from users and disappearing (correct)

A deliberate or reckless exit.

Tip

If your design makes a rug pull technically easy, users have to trust you completely. Design so that they do not have to.

Check what you just learned

1. Nobody legitimate will ever ask for:
  • Your recovery phrase (correct)
  • Your public address
  • Your username
  • Your feedback

Never share it.
keyPoints: Fake tokens, rug pulls, honeypots and phishing are common.
Limit your own powers so users do not have to trust you blindly.

topics.title: A launch checklist
topics.html:
Before launch
ItemDone when
Purpose and designA one-page specification exists and a token is truly needed
TestsUnit, fuzz and invariant tests pass, with high coverage
ReviewAn independent security review is finished and findings are fixed
LegalAdvice has been taken for the relevant countries
ControlsOwner powers sit in a multi-signature wallet; time-lock if upgradeable
TransparencySource is verified; allocation, vesting and powers are published
DisclosureRisks are written in plain language
SupportOfficial channels are announced and monitored
At launch
ItemWhy
Start on a test network, then launch with a small capLimits harm from undiscovered bugs
Publish the official address in one trusted placeReduces fake-token confusion
Monitor transfers and admin actionsCatch unusual activity fast
Have an incident planKnow who pauses and communicates

Cap and expected loss

Change the launch cap and the chance of a serious bug to see the expected loss. A teaching model with made-up numbers.

Adjust Launch cap (rupees), Chance of a serious bug (%) and see Expected loss (rupees) change.

Check what you just learned

1. Why launch with a small cap?
  • To look modest
  • To limit the harm from undiscovered bugs (correct)
  • To save gas
  • To avoid audits

Start small.

Check what you just learned

1. After launching you should:
  • Stop paying attention
  • Remove the source
  • Monitor and have an incident plan (correct)
  • Hide the owner

Operations matter.

Key terms: flip and sort

Security (in law)
A regulated kind of investment instrument
Rug pull
An exit scam draining users' value
Honeypot
A token that cannot be sold
Phishing
Tricking users into harmful actions
Disclosure
A plain statement of facts and risks
Launch cap
A small first limit on supply or deposits
keyPoints: Design, test, review, take legal advice, then launch small.
Publish the official address and monitor after launch.
